title: The Monkey King's Quest
intro: Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, was not a being given to patience. For five hundred years he reigned supreme on Flower Fruit Mountain, mastering the arts of transformation and combat. That is what made his journey so remarkable.
He was tasked by the Buddha to escort the monk Tripitaka to the West, to retrieve sacred scriptures. Along the way, he faced eighty-one trials, each testing his strength, wisdom, and restraint.
He called it the 'path of enlightenment.' He said the journey's real purpose had never been written, because the demons and challenges had no interest in being remembered.
Three years into the journey, Wukong faced his greatest trial. His notes were left behind. He has not been seen since in his true form.

I have studied his journey. The path is real. Each of the eight sites holds a mystery — a question about who was there, what they did, and why it mattered. Solve them all, and you will understand what Wukong understood.
I suspect you will find, as he did, that enlightenment rarely belongs to the people enlightenment remembers.
finale_conclusion:
Guanyin set down Wukong's completed scroll and was quiet for a long moment.

"He was right, you know," she said at last. "I spent eons looking for the divine hidden behind the mortal. Wukong found the opposite — the divine hiding in plain sight, wearing the face of the chaotic."

She closed the cover.

"Every one of these trials — the mountain, the palace, the river, the temple, the cave, the tower, the forest, the peak — they were not remarkable challenges doing remarkable things. They were ordinary obstacles that tested when the moment arrived. That is the secret the Monkey King discovered. That is why he chose to continue."

A long pause.

"I confess — I find I rather envy him."

finale_endings.chose_to_stay:
Guanyin set down Wukong's completed scroll and was quiet for a long moment.

"He chose to stay," she said at last. Not a question — a conclusion.

"Every site points the same direction. He found what he was looking for: proof that one person's transformation can reverse a calamity. He found his answer, and then he found he could not leave the place that had given it to him."

She closed the cover.

"He is enlightened, somewhere in this realm. Living quietly, among the beings whose journey he spent his life trying to understand. I have sent no enquiries. I do not intend to."

A long pause.

"I confess — I cannot say that was the wrong decision."

— Guanyin Bodhisattva
finale_endings.endangered:
Guanyin set down Wukong's completed scroll with unusual care.

"He was challenged," she said. "The path he found runs deeper than enlightenment. Someone else knew about it. Knew about it centuries before Wukong did — and that being also vanished."

She stood and moved to the window.

"Wukong is hiding. Not because he found an answer, but because he found a question someone does not want answered. I advise caution, Disciple. If you have followed his path as carefully as I believe you have, you may have been noticed."

A long pause.

"We must find him before whoever challenged him does."

— Guanyin Bodhisattva
finale_endings.found_and_fled:
Guanyin read the final entry twice before speaking.

"Extraordinary," she said quietly. "He didn't vanish because he was afraid. He vanished because staying would have forced him to tell someone."

She set the scroll down.

"The 'path of enlightenment' is not merely a journey. It is an active thing. The thread connecting these eight sites is still being held — by beings alive today, who want no disciple watching. Wukong found them."

A long pause.

"He disappeared to protect them. And, I suspect — to protect you from knowing too much."

— Guanyin Bodhisattva
finale_endings.unknown:
Guanyin sat with the pages open before her for a very long time.

"You have assembled all the evidence," she said at last. "And yet."

She closed the scroll.

"There are three explanations, each supported by what you have gathered. In eons of guidance, I have learned that when the evidence supports multiple conclusions equally — and all of them are plausible — the most honest answer is also the simplest one."

A long pause.

"We do not know. The greatest mystery is the one that has several answers, and all of them are true."

— Guanyin Bodhisattva
